content: Maternal nutrient supplementation has been explored as a potential intervention to improve fetal growth when it is suspected to be impaired. Various nutrients, including carbohydrates and amino acids, have been proposed as therapeutic options for addressing this issue. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the effects of maternal nutrient supplementation on fetal growth and perinatal outcomes in cases of suspected fetal growth restriction. To achieve this, a search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of March 2010. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared nutrient supplementation to either placebo or no treatment in cases of suspected impaired fetal growth. The quality of the included trials was assessed to ensure reliability. Four studies, involving a total of 165 women, were included in the analysis. However, these trials were limited by their small sample sizes and methodological weaknesses. One finding was that the use of carnitine supplementation was associated with a shorter duration of pregnancy after enrollment, with a mean reduction of 2.12 weeks (95% confidence interval: -3.58 to -0.66 weeks). Additionally, intraamniotic administration of nutrients was linked to higher birth weights (mean birth weight: 2575 g, standard deviation: 780 g) compared to intravenous administration (mean birth weight: 2080 g, standard deviation: 457 g). No other significant differences in outcomes were observed. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of nutrient supplementation as a treatment for suspected impaired fetal growth. The small sample sizes of the included studies limit the ability to draw definitive conclusions regarding clinical outcomes.
